pages.title: Model Essay 6: Spending on Space Exploration
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Essay: Should Money Be Spent on Space Exploration? | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 opinion essay on government spending on space exploration, with a plan, the model answer and notes on disagreeing with a premise.
pages.keywords: IELTS space exploration essay, IELTS agree or disagree essay, IELTS opinion essay model answer

hero.text: Question type: opinion. This one rewards a candidate who is willing to attack the assumption buried in the question.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Governments should stop spending money on space exploration and use it to solve problems on Earth instead.*
**Do you agree or disagree?**
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.title: You are allowed to challenge the question
text: This statement contains an unstated assumption: that the money saved would in fact be spent on the problems mentioned, and that the two compete for the same funds.

Examining an assumption like this is not evasion, provided you still answer the question. It is one of the clearest signals of a Band 8 or 9 Task Response - but only if you then commit to a position. Identifying the flaw and refusing to answer scores badly.

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Introduction
State the position: **disagree**, and flag that the statement rests on a false comparison.
Body 1
The strongest form of the opposing case, conceded properly: urgent needs, real opportunity cost.
Body 2
The scale objection: space budgets are small relative to the problems they are compared with, so the trade-off is largely illusory.
Body 3
The direct-benefit argument: much of what space programmes produce is used on Earth - weather, navigation, climate observation.
Conclusion
Reframe: the real question is not space versus Earth, but whether public money is spent well.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (292 words)
items.prompt: Governments should stop spending money on space exploration and use it to solve problems on Earth instead. Do you agree or disagree?
sample: The argument for stopping space exploration is a powerful one. It seems wrong to send equipment to other planets while people on this one lack clean water. I disagree with it all the same, mainly because the comparison it depends on is not a real one.

The case deserves to be stated fairly first. Public money is limited, every choice means giving something else up, and the needs it is compared with are urgent and concrete. Housing, medicine and clean water help people now, in a way that a distant scientific result does not. Anyone who dismisses that is not taking the question seriously.

The difficulty is that the two things are not really competing for the same money. National space budgets are a very small part of government spending, much smaller than most people imagine when they picture the choice. Closing them completely would make very little difference to the problems in question. Meanwhile, far larger sums are lost through poor purchasing or spent on paying interest on debt. If the real concern is that public money should go where it does most good, space is a strange place to begin.

There is also a more direct objection. Much of what space programmes produce is not about other planets at all. Weather forecasting, satellite navigation, global communications and, most importantly, the measurement of our own climate all depend on systems built and maintained by space agencies. A great deal of the money described as spent on space is in fact spent on understanding this planet, and it would have to be spent again under another name.
In my view the question is put the wrong way round. What matters is not whether money is spent above the atmosphere or below it, but whether it is spent well.
notes: **The position is in the first paragraph**, with the reason previewed: *the comparison it depends on is not a real one*. The reader knows the shape of the essay immediately.
**The concession is generous and raises the stakes.** *Anyone who dismisses that is not taking the question seriously* obliges the essay to argue properly rather than sneer at the other side.

**The scale argument avoids inventing a number.** *A very small part of government spending*, *much smaller than most people imagine* - defensible, and no fabricated figure. A candidate writing *0.48% of GDP* gains nothing and might be wrong.
**The strongest point is placed third**, not first. Building towards the best argument is more persuasive than leading with it.
**The conclusion reframes rather than repeats.** It turns a yes-or-no question into a better question, which reads as judgement.
**One sentence does a paragraph's work:** *If the real concern is that public money should go where it does most good, space is a strange place to begin.*
**292 words**, sentences of about sixteen words. Band 7 to 7.5 - the argument is what scores here, not the vocabulary.

items.term: The case deserves to be stated fairly first.
items.def: Announces a concession and commits you to making it properly.

items.term: the comparison it depends on is not a real one
items.def: Challenges a premise in nine words.

items.term: is a strange place to begin
items.def: Dismissive without being rude - a register that scores well.

items.term: it would have to be spent again under another name
items.def: Shows that an apparent saving is not one.

items.term: the question is put the wrong way round
items.def: Save this for a conclusion where you have earned it by arguing the point first.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you commit to a position, or only criticise the question?
Did you state the opposing case in its strongest form?
Did you avoid inventing budget figures?
Does your conclusion add something, rather than repeat the introduction?
Are you between 260 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Now try this variation
text: *Money spent on the arts would be better spent on public services.* **Do you agree or disagree?**

The same false-comparison move is available. But be careful: the scale argument is weaker here, because arts budgets and public service budgets are drawn from the same local pots far more often. Test whether the move actually works before you use it.

pages.title: Model Essay 7: Museums, Tourists and Local People
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Essay: Should Museums Serve Tourists or Locals? | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 discussion essay on whether museums should serve tourists or local people, with a plan, model answer and marking notes.
pages.keywords: IELTS museums essay, IELTS discuss both views model answer, IELTS tourism essay task 2

hero.text: Question type: discussion. A narrow topic, which is harder than a broad one - there is nowhere to hide behind general statements.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Some people think that museums should be designed mainly to attract visitors from other countries. Others believe their main purpose is to serve the people who live locally.*
**Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.**
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Introduction
Note that the two aims conflict less often than the question implies, but that where they do conflict, one must win. Position: **local first**.
Body 1
The tourist case: revenue, and the fact that visitor income often funds everything else the museum does.
Body 2
The local case: a museum that no local person visits twice becomes a spectacle rather than an institution - and the difference shows in what it collects.
Body 3
My position and the practical test: who does the museum serve on a wet Tuesday in February?
Conclusion
Serving locals well is what makes a museum worth travelling to.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (288 words)
items.prompt: Some people think that museums should be designed mainly to attract visitors from other countries. Others believe their main purpose is to serve the people who live locally. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
sample: Most museums manage to serve both tourists and local people without much trouble. The two aims do pull apart at the edges, however, over what is collected, how it is displayed and what it costs to enter. Where they do conflict, I believe the local audience should come first.

The argument for designing around visitors is mainly financial, and it is not a weak one. International tourists pay entrance fees, buy things in the shop and eat in the cafe. In many museums that income is what pays for the conservation work, the archive and the free schools programme. A museum that ignored visitors completely might be admirable in principle and unable to open on Mondays. There is also a fair argument that a country's major collections are part of how it presents itself to the world.

The argument for the local audience is less about money and more about what a museum is for. A place designed for people passing through once will drift towards the famous, the photogenic and the easily explained, because that is what a single short visit rewards. A museum built for people who might return twenty times has to be deeper than that. It has to keep material of local importance that no tourist has heard of, change its displays, and expect its visitors to know something already.

My own test is a simple one. Who is the museum for on a wet Tuesday in February, when there are no tourists at all? An institution with no good answer to that has become an attraction rather than a museum.
In the end the two aims are not really opposed. Museums that take their own communities seriously tend to be exactly the ones that visitors travel a long way to see.
notes: **The introduction refuses the false opposition** and then narrows to where the conflict is real. That is more precise than accepting the question's framing wholesale, and it is done in two sentences without dodging.
**Both views are argued generously.** *Admirable in principle and unable to open on Mondays* concedes the financial case with a touch of wit rather than grudgingly.
**The third paragraph explains a mechanism** - how designing for one-time visitors changes what a museum collects. That causal chain is what makes the argument feel earned rather than asserted.
**The wet-Tuesday test is the memorable move.** A concrete test does more persuasive work than an abstract principle, and it gives the opinion paragraph something to be about.
**The conclusion resolves rather than restates**, arguing that the two aims meet in the end - a genuine step beyond the introduction.
**Vocabulary is exact rather than showy:** *drift towards*, *the photogenic and the easily explained*, *an attraction rather than a museum*.
**297 words**, both views at similar length, opinion clearly stated. Band 7 to 7.5.

items.term: The two aims do pull apart at the edges, however
items.def: Concedes that a conflict is limited while keeping it real enough to write about.

items.term: might be admirable in principle and unable to open on Mondays
items.def: Concession with a dry edge. Register like this is credited under Lexical Resource.

items.term: My own test is a simple one.
items.def: Introduces a concrete criterion rather than an abstract claim.

items.term: has become an attraction rather than a museum
items.def: Draws a distinction between two words the reader assumed were the same.

items.term: In the end the two aims are not really opposed.
items.def: Resolves a discussion essay without pretending the disagreement never existed.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you give both views similar space?
Did you state an opinion clearly rather than implying it?
Did you find a concrete test or example, rather than staying abstract throughout?
Did your conclusion add something?
Are you between 260 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Now try this variation
text: *Some people believe historic city centres should be preserved exactly as they are. Others think they should be redeveloped to meet modern needs.* **Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.**
Try to find a concrete test of your own, as the wet-Tuesday question does here. Abstract principles are easy to write and easy to forget; a test forces you to be specific.

pages.title: Model Essay 8: Plastic Waste
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Essay: Plastic Waste Causes and Solutions | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 causes and solutions essay on plastic waste, with a plan, the model answer and notes on avoiding the recycling cliche.
pages.keywords: IELTS plastic waste essay, IELTS causes and solutions essay, IELTS environment essay model answer
pages.kicker: Model essay 8 of 10: causes and solutions

hero.text: Question type: causes and solutions. Environment questions attract the most memorised writing of any topic, which makes an unexpected point unusually valuable here.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *The amount of plastic waste produced worldwide continues to increase.*
**What are the causes of this, and what solutions can you suggest?**
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.title: The most over-used essay in IELTS
text: Environmental questions produce more memorised answers than any other topic. *We should raise awareness, the government should impose strict laws, and people should recycle more* appears in thousands of scripts a week and is worth very little, because it names no mechanism and could be attached to any problem at all.

The essay below deliberately avoids all three. Notice that it treats recycling as **part of the problem**, which is both defensible and the sort of thing an examiner has not read forty times that morning.

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Introduction
Signal both halves and preview the argument: plastic is cheap and its costs are paid by someone else.
Body 1
Causes: plastic is extraordinarily cheap to produce and the cost of disposal falls on no one who makes the decision. Plus the shift to single-use packaging.
Body 2
Why recycling has not solved it: much plastic is not economically recyclable, and the belief that it is has reduced pressure to use less.
Body 3
Solutions that follow: put disposal cost onto producers, and require reusable packaging where it is practical.
Conclusion
The principle: make the person who chooses the packaging pay for its disposal.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (295 words)
items.prompt: The amount of plastic waste produced worldwide continues to increase. What are the causes of this, and what solutions can you suggest?
sample: Plastic waste keeps increasing for a straightforward economic reason. Plastic is very cheap to make, and almost none of the cost of dealing with it afterwards falls on the person who chooses to use it. Any solution that does not change that will not work.

The first cause is the material itself. Plastic is light, strong, clean and extremely cheap, so for a manufacturer choosing packaging it is nearly always the sensible choice. The second cause is a change in the way goods are sold. Food that was once bought loose, or delivered in containers that were returned and refilled, now arrives individually wrapped. The growth of home delivery has added a second layer of packaging around the first. Neither change happened because customers asked for plastic; both happened because of cost and convenience elsewhere in the chain.

It is worth asking why recycling has not solved this, because a great deal of hope has been placed on it. Much plastic packaging is made of mixed or coloured plastics that are not worth separating, so it is exported, buried or burned whichever bin it was put in. The more serious problem is that believing plastic is recyclable has taken the pressure off using less of it. A recycling symbol reassures the person buying the product, and that reassurance is exactly what reduces the demand for change.

The solutions follow from the causes. Producers should pay the full cost of disposing of the packaging they choose, so that the cheapest option for them becomes the cheapest option for everyone else. Where refillable systems are practical, as they are for drinks, cleaning products and dry goods, they should be required rather than merely encouraged.
The principle is simple. Whoever chooses the packaging should pay for getting rid of it.
notes: **Causes and solutions are genuinely linked.** The fourth paragraph solves the exact problem named in the first - that disposal costs fall on someone other than the person choosing. Most essays fail this by proposing solutions unconnected to their own causes.

**The recycling paragraph is the best idea in the essay**, and it is the opposite of the expected one. Arguing that a supposed remedy is part of the problem is memorable and shows independent thought.
**No *raise awareness*, no *strict laws*, no *people should recycle more*.** Every proposal names a mechanism and says who acts.
**Causes are explained rather than listed.** The second cause is not *there is more packaging now*; it is an account of why there is, and who drove it.
**Honest about uncertainty:** *much plastic packaging*, *where refillable systems are practical*. Qualifiers of this kind are more convincing than invented percentages.
**The conclusion is a single-sentence principle.** After a dense essay, brevity reads as confidence.
**297 words.** Band 7 to 7.5, and note that the whole essay uses ordinary vocabulary.

items.term: almost none of the cost falls on the person who chooses to use it
items.def: States an externality in plain English. Transfers to pollution, traffic, water use and much else.

items.term: Any solution that does not change that will not work.
items.def: Sets a test your own solutions then have to pass - a useful discipline.

items.term: It is worth asking why X has not solved this
items.def: Introduces a paragraph that challenges an assumption the reader holds.

items.term: that reassurance is exactly what reduces the demand for change
items.def: A counter-intuitive causal claim in plain words.

items.term: should be required rather than merely encouraged
items.def: Distinguishes two strengths of policy - far more precise than *the government should take action*.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Does each solution address a cause you actually named?
Did you avoid *raise awareness* and *impose strict laws*?
Does every proposal say who does what?
Did you explain why your causes came about, or only state them?
Are you between 260 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Now try this variation
text: *A large proportion of the food produced in the world is thrown away.* **What are the causes, and what could be done to reduce it?**
The same economic frame works: who decides, and who pays. Try to find the equivalent of the recycling point - the widely praised remedy that quietly makes the problem easier to ignore.

pages.title: Model Essay 9: Ageing Populations
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Essay: Ageing Populations Advantages and Disadvantages | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 advantages and disadvantages essay on ageing populations, with a plan, the model answer and notes on handling a topic you may know little about.
pages.keywords: IELTS ageing population essay, IELTS advantages disadvantages model answer, IELTS task 2 society essay
pages.kicker: Model essay 9 of 10: advantages and disadvantages

hero.text: Question type: advantages and disadvantages, without an *outweigh*. Read the instruction: this one asks you to discuss, not to decide.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *In many countries, people are living considerably longer than they did in the past, and the proportion of older people in the population is rising.*
**Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this development.**
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.title: What to do when you know little about the topic
text: You are not being marked on knowledge. Nobody expects a candidate to have read demographic research, and no examiner checks your facts.

What you can always do is **reason from the general to the particular**. If more people are old, then more people are retired, then fewer workers support more pensioners, then either taxes rise or the retirement age does. That chain is available to anyone who thinks for two minutes, and it produces a better essay than a half-remembered statistic.
The one thing to avoid is inventing numbers. *By 2050 there will be 2.1 billion people over 60* earns nothing even if it happens to be right.

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Introduction
Note that this is a symptom of success, which is the framing most essays miss. Signal both sides.
Body 1
Advantages: longer healthy working lives, accumulated skill, and unpaid work - especially childcare - that makes other people's employment possible.
Body 2
Disadvantages: the dependency arithmetic, and the concentration of healthcare cost in the final years.
Body 3 (short)
The observation that ties them together: which side dominates depends almost entirely on whether the added years are healthy ones.
Conclusion
Balanced, because the instruction is *discuss* - but with the healthy-years point restated as the thing that decides it.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (286 words)
items.prompt: In many countries, people are living considerably longer than they did in the past, and the proportion of older people in the population is rising. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this development.
sample: It is worth beginning by noticing what an ageing population actually shows. It is the result of better medicine, safer work, cleaner water and fewer children dying. In other words it is a sign of success, even though it is almost always discussed as a crisis. It does, however, bring real difficulties alongside its benefits.

The advantages are easy to overlook. People who stay healthy into their seventies can carry on working, and they bring judgement and experience that cannot be gained quickly. In fields such as medicine, teaching and law, the most valuable people are rarely the youngest. Older people also do an enormous amount of unpaid work that never appears in any economic figure. Grandparents who provide regular childcare are, in effect, paying for the employment of the generation below them, and communities depend heavily on retired volunteers for tasks nobody is paid to do.

The disadvantages are mainly a matter of arithmetic. If a smaller working population has to support a larger retired one, then either taxes rise, retirement comes later, or pensions and services are cut. All three are politically difficult. Healthcare costs are also concentrated heavily in the last years of life, so a society with more people at that stage will spend much more on medicine however efficient its system is.

What decides which side matters more is not how long people live but how well. Extra years spent working, helping and living independently are a clear gain. Extra years spent frail and dependent are a clear cost.
The development therefore brings genuine advantages and genuine difficulties, and the balance between them depends far less on how long people live than on how healthy they are while doing so.
notes: **The instruction is *discuss*, not *do the advantages outweigh*, so the essay stays balanced** and does not force a verdict. Matching the answer to the exact wording is the whole of Task Response.
**The opening reframes the topic** - success, not crisis - which immediately separates this from the standard treatment.

**The advantages paragraph finds the point most candidates miss:** unpaid childcare as a subsidy to the working generation. Looking for the effect that is invisible in the obvious framing is the most reliable way to produce an original paragraph.

**The disadvantages are handled by reasoning, not data.** *Either taxes rise, retirement comes later, or pensions and services are cut* is a complete argument derived from first principles, and needs no statistics.
**The short fourth paragraph introduces the distinction that organises everything** - healthy years against dependent years - and it is placed late so the conclusion can use it.
**The conclusion is balanced but not empty.** It refuses a verdict, as instructed, while still saying what the answer depends on.
**300 words.** Band 7 to 7.5.

items.term: It is worth beginning by noticing what X actually shows.
items.def: Opens by reframing, and warns the reader that the obvious reading is about to be questioned.

items.term: a sign of success, even though it is almost always discussed as a crisis
items.def: Contrasts what something is with how it is described.

items.term: The advantages are easy to overlook.
items.def: A topic sentence that promises something non-obvious.

items.term: are, in effect, paying for
items.def: *In effect* lets you make a strong economic claim about something that involves no money.

items.term: depends far less on how long people live than on how healthy they are
items.def: A *less X than Y* construction to close on, at the point the examiner forms a final impression.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you check whether the question asked you to *discuss* or to *decide*?
Did you find at least one advantage that is not obvious?
Did you reason from first principles rather than reaching for statistics?
Did you avoid inventing figures?
Are you between 260 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Now try this variation
text: *In many countries, more and more people are choosing to live alone.* **Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?**
Note the change of instruction - this one wants a verdict. Practise spotting that difference at the planning stage, because it is the single easiest band to lose.

pages.title: Model Essay 10: Traditional Skills
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Essay: Why Are Traditional Skills Disappearing? | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 two-part question essay on disappearing traditional skills, with a plan, the model answer and notes on answering both parts.
pages.keywords: IELTS traditional skills essay, IELTS two part question model answer, IELTS culture essay task 2

hero.text: Question type: two-part. The second half asks what should be done - which means the essay has to commit to something specific.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *In many countries, traditional crafts and skills are disappearing as older generations pass away.*
**Why is this happening, and what, if anything, should be done about it?**
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.title: Notice the words *if anything*
text: *What, if anything, should be done* explicitly permits you to argue that **nothing** should be done, or that only some things are worth saving. The question is inviting a discriminating answer rather than a list of preservation measures.
Small qualifiers of this kind appear often, and reading past them is how candidates end up answering a slightly different question from the one asked.

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Introduction
Answer both halves in a sentence each. Position: save selectively, not comprehensively.
Body 1 (why)
Two causes: the economic one (machines make the product more cheaply), and the transmission one (these skills pass by apprenticeship, and one missed generation breaks the chain permanently).
Body 2 (what)
The distinction that does the work: preserving a *product* is sentimental; preserving *knowledge that cannot be reconstructed* is not.
Body 3
Concretely: fund apprenticeships where the knowledge is genuinely irrecoverable; record the rest properly while people can still demonstrate it.
Conclusion
Restate the criterion - can it be relearned from a record, or only from a person?

items.label: Original RCF model answer (297 words)
items.prompt: In many countries, traditional crafts and skills are disappearing as older generations pass away. Why is this happening, and what, if anything, should be done about it?
sample: Traditional crafts are disappearing mainly because the work they once did is now done more cheaply by other means, and because the way they are passed on is unusually fragile. I do not think everything can or should be saved, but one particular kind of knowledge is worth real effort.

The economic cause is simple. A machine-made basket costs a fraction of a hand-made one and does the same job, so demand falls away. A craft that cannot support a household will not attract anyone willing to learn it. The second cause matters more and is mentioned less. These skills are passed on by watching and correction over several years, not by instruction, and much of what the expert knows cannot be put into words. Knowing the moment a piece of wood is ready, or the sound that shows the temperature is right, lives in people rather than in books. If one generation does not learn it, there is nobody left to demonstrate it, and the loss is permanent in a way that losing a written technique is not.

That difference seems to me the right basis for deciding what to do. Keeping a craft alive simply because it is old, when the object it makes is worse and more expensive than the alternative, is sentimental and unlikely to survive once the funding stops. Keeping knowledge that cannot be recovered once it is gone is a completely different matter.

In practice this suggests two things. Where a skill is genuinely irrecoverable and still has a living practitioner, paid apprenticeships are worth the cost, because a person is the only possible record. Where it is not, careful recording, filmed and detailed and made while the expert can still be questioned, is a reasonable and far cheaper alternative.
The test is simple. Could this be learned again from a record, or only from a person?
notes: **Both halves of the question are answered in the introduction**, and the position responds to the *if anything* qualifier: not everything should be saved.
**The second cause is the strong one and the essay says so** - *matters more and is mentioned less*. Ranking your own points is a Band 7 and above habit.
**Tacit knowledge is explained without the term:** *the moment a piece of wood is ready*, *the sound that shows the temperature is right*. Two concrete examples do more than a technical word would.
**The essay produces a criterion rather than a list**, and then applies it. That is the difference between an argument and a set of suggestions.
**The proposals are specific:** paid apprenticeships where the knowledge is irrecoverable, recording where it is not, with a reason for choosing between them.
**A one-line conclusion.** After a densely argued essay, a single-sentence test lands hard and reads as confidence rather than as running out of time.
**303 words.** Band 7 to 7.5, with plain vocabulary throughout.

items.term: The second cause matters more and is mentioned less.
items.def: Ranks your points explicitly. Costs five words and lifts the paragraph.

items.term: lives in people rather than in books
items.def: A short phrase carrying the paragraph's whole idea.

items.term: is sentimental and unlikely to survive once the funding stops
items.def: Rejects a position on two grounds at once - one about value, one about practicality.

items.term: a person is the only possible record
items.def: A metaphor that argues rather than decorates.

items.term: Could this be learned again from a record, or only from a person?
items.def: Ending on a question is risky, but effective when the question is the essay's actual criterion.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you answer both halves at similar length?
Did you notice *if anything* and allow yourself to be selective?
Did you produce a criterion, or only a list of suggestions?
Are your suggestions specific enough to say who does what?
Are you between 260 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Now try this variation
text: *Some languages are spoken by only a few hundred people and are likely to disappear within a generation.* **Why does this matter, and what, if anything, should be done?**

The same criterion transfers almost exactly - what can be reconstructed from a record, and what only lives in people. Notice that it transfers because the underlying structure is the same, not because the topic is. That is what studying a model essay is for.
